Pairing Signals

L1 · Bound The clean signal does not have to be abandoned. Both platforms already combine signals in a way that suits this problem. The Kubernetes autoscaler, given several metrics, “takes the maximum scale recommended for each metric and sets the workload to that size”[6] . AWS target tracking with several policies “will scale out the Auto Scaling group if any of the target tracking policies are ready to scale out”, and scales in only when all of them agree[2] .

L1 · Bound Pair the first-attempt signal with ingress rate, at the same target, and take the larger recommendation. In a healthy service there are no retries, the two signals read the same, and the pair behaves like the clean signal alone. In a failing one the ingress signal reads A times higher and wins, and Corollary 5 applies: capacity rises until equals the target, and the service recovers. Once attempts succeed, the retries stop, ingress falls back to demand, and the pair releases the extra pods. The clean signal keeps the precision it was chosen for, and the dirty one supplies the power it lacks.

L2 · Fit The pair has a price, and it is paid only on the worst day. During a failure it orders A times the needed capacity, which in a stack with an amplification of nine is nine times the need. A replica ceiling, or a cluster without room for that capacity, takes the escape away. Pairing with CPU instead also escapes, more slowly and with more overshoot, for the reasons the first post of this series gave. What pairing cannot do is repair a service whose amplification is so high that the capacity to clear its debt does not exist.

L2 · Fit Huang and coauthors left a question open: “Whether the current autoscaling techniques can scale up fast enough to avert a metastable failure requires further research.” They also noted that autoscaling “does not necessarily prevent metastable failures”. The corollary answers part of the first question, and the answer is about the signal rather than the speed. The first-attempt scaler is the fastest of the three. It reached its capacity in 120 seconds, as fast as ingress and nearly three times faster than CPU, and it is the only one that stays trapped. A scaler can be fast enough and still never get out, because the capacity it is fast to reach is the wrong capacity.

L2 · Fit One Bit per Dead Time priced the target as an information rate. Corollary 4 adds a second price. With retries in the system, the target also sets whether the service has a second, permanent state. A team that raises a first-attempt target from 30% to 50% to save pods has moved its service from a recovery of fifteen minutes to no recovery at all. Nothing in steady-state operation will tell it so.

A Limit on the Self-Verification Rule

This blog has argued, more than once, that a system cannot grade its own homework. A check is honest only if it draws on something the thing it checks could not also have corrupted. The first-attempt signal looks like the perfect application of that rule. It is measured at the edge, by clients, independent of the service’s own state. CPU is the opposite, a number the service produces about itself.

L2 · Fit In this model, the self-produced metric recovered and the independent one did not. The rule survives this, and The Shared Ancestor Problem already said why. Its criterion for a check has two conditions, independence and power, and it warned that “independence without power certifies a coin flip”. The first-attempt signal is independent of the service’s state and has no power over the quantity that matters, because the debt is part of that state. CPU fails independence and has the power. Ingress rate has some of each: it is measured outside the pods, and it includes the retries that carry the debt into view.

L2 · Fit Set beside the two posts before it, this result completes a pattern. The saturated CPU metric of One Bit per Dead Time could not see the size of an overload. The backlog of The Delay a Window Demands could see the size, and it carried the memory of every shortfall into the controller. The clean demand signal has neither problem, and it cannot see state at all. Each signal is blind to something, and each blindness is a property of what the signal is defined to count, not of how carefully it is measured. Ashby’s requisite variety, which the first post used as an analogy, applies here as one too. A regulator cannot counter a disturbance its channel does not carry, and the debt is a disturbance the clean channel was built to exclude.

L2 · Fit The lesson sharpens the rule rather than retiring it. A signal must be independent of the errors it is meant to catch, and it must see the quantity it governs. When a service’s load includes its own history, a signal that is independent of that history is also blind to it. Cleaning a signal of everything the system did to itself can clean away the thing that decides whether it recovers.

What Is Known and What Is Added

L1 · Bound The pattern is established, and this post adds to it rather than discovering it. Bronson and coauthors named metastable failures, their trigger and their sustaining effect, and their retry example contains the threshold of Proposition 6. Huang and coauthors measured how often retries sustain them and discussed autoscaling as a partial mitigation. Alvaro and five coauthors model request-response servers as continuous-time Markov chains and compute recovery times “either exactly by solving a linear system or approximately through estimates of eigenvalues”[7] . Habibi and four coauthors built a queueing model, MSF-Model, to “characterize and predict metastable failures” in replicated storage[8] .

L2 · Fit Three things were not found in the sources read. The first is the closed-form recovery time of Proposition 7, with its divergence as tied to this blog’s definitions of metastable and bistable. The second is Corollary 4, the trap condition for an autoscaler whose signal excludes the debt, with its threshold of one over the amplification. The third is the three-signal comparison, which shows that the cleanest and fastest signal is the one that stays trapped. They are offered as this post’s contribution, with the usual caution about absence from the sources read.

What the Model Leaves Out

L2 · Fit The largest omission is the one the reversal condition names. A service that propagates deadlines, or that cancels work when its client disconnects, does not serve abandoned attempts. Its debt is close to zero, the amplification of Definition 8 no longer turns into work, and the trap condition does not apply in this form. Retries still add attempts, and a service that drops them late still pays for part of each one. The protection is partial in practice, and it depends on where in the stack the work is dropped.

L2 · Fit Client-side circuit breakers act on the amplification directly. A breaker that opens when most calls fail stops retries and first attempts alike, which lowers A to below one while it is open. That can break the trap, at the price of failing every request fast instead of slowly. The model has no breakers.

L1 · Bound Client-side limits are a gentler form of the same lever, and they are deployed. The AWS SDKs’ standard retry mode keeps a retry quota, “a token bucket that deducts tokens for each retry and replenishes tokens when requests succeed”. When the tokens run out, “the SDK returns the error without retrying”[9] . Its default of three attempts is the two retries of this post’s specimen. Envoy’s adaptive concurrency filter “dynamically adjusts the allowed number of requests that can be outstanding” to a cluster from sampled latencies, updated every 100 milliseconds in its example configuration[10] . Netflix’s concurrency-limits library borrows TCP congestion control for the same purpose and lists among its ground rules that “we can use timeouts and rejected requests to aggressively back off”[11] .

L2 · Fit Each of these lowers only if what it refuses stays refused. A limiter that rejects a request has removed one attempt. If a layer above it retries the rejection, whether an SDK wrapper, a gateway or a user pressing reload, the attempt comes back and the amplification is unchanged. The rejection has only moved where the debt waits. Envoy’s documentation shows how easily this happens. It expects more 503 responses while the filter measures its baseline latency and states that “it is recommended to enable retries for resets/503s”. That advice is aimed at the measurement window, when other hosts still have room, but the same retries fire during an overload, when none do. A limiter lowers the amplification the trap condition reads only when its rejections are terminal, or are charged against the same retry budget as timeouts.

L2 · Fit The fluid model and the request-level model agree to within about 2% on recovery times, but neither has realistic service times. The fluid model has no distribution at all, and the request-level model uses exponential service. Heavy-tailed service times make waits more variable, so some requests time out even below the trigger of Proposition 8, and they could produce triggers of their own. None appeared in the request-level runs up to 95% utilization, and none could appear in a model whose service times have no tail.

L2 · Fit Finally, the model’s clients are perfectly persistent: every timeout produces a retry, up to the cap. Real users also give up and leave. A user who abandons for good lowers the amplification, which helps the service and hurts the business. The model’s numbers are therefore the worst case for the service and say nothing about the demand that never comes back.

The Binding Constraint, in Sequence

L2 · Fit The Constraint Sequence Framework asks which constraint binds first. For retry debt the amplification binds first, because it sets the threshold every other choice is measured against, and it is set by policies spread across every client and layer. The signal binds second, because it decides whether the autoscaler can see the debt at all. The target binds third: given a blind signal, it decides which side of the threshold the service lives on. Nobody sets the trigger; it is the event that eventually arrives.

L2 · Fit The sequence says where to look first. A team that finds its service trapped will be tempted to tune the autoscaler, which is the third constraint, or to add backoff, which changes none of them. The first constraint is the amplification, and it is usually set in client libraries the service team does not own.

What This Post Did Not Claim

Where Each Claim Holds

Claim. A failed service stays failed if and only if .

  • Assumption: first-in-first-out service, clients that retry at once on timeout, and servers that complete abandoned work.
  • Failure mode: deadline propagation, request cancellation or last-in-first-out service drop abandoned work and remove the debt; the condition then does not apply.

Claim. Recovery takes about for a long spike, less the ramp before the first timeout.

  • Assumption: a fluid queue in which retries stop the moment the wait falls below the timeout.
  • Failure mode: retries already in flight at that moment, or bursty arrivals, blur the phase boundaries; in the runs the full form stays within 1.2% of the fluid model.

Claim. A scaler on a debt-excluding signal is trapped when its target is at least 1/A.

  • Assumption: the scaler reaches its target capacity, and the trigger occurs before or while it does.
  • Failure mode: a replica ceiling below the target capacity, or a signal that partly includes retries, changes the effective utilization.

Claim. A trigger is required.

  • Assumption: the request-level model with Poisson arrivals and exponential service, run for 20,000 seconds.
  • Failure mode: heavier-tailed service times or bursty arrivals could produce their own triggers; none appeared in these runs up to 95% utilization.

Reversal condition. The advice of this post is to scale on a signal that sees the debt, or to remove the debt. It reverses when the service drops abandoned work. With deadline propagation or cancellation, the debt does not exist, the first-attempt signal measures the whole load, and its cleanliness becomes the advantage it was supposed to be.

What Is Not Claimed

The fluid model and the request-level model agree to within about 2% on recovery times, and both use simple service times and perfectly persistent clients. The thresholds of Propositions 6 to 8 and Corollaries 4 and 5 follow from the fluid arithmetic. The specific recovery times, the trace of the trap and the comparison of the three signals belong to the specimen. They move when its timeout, its retry counts or its dead time move.

It has not been claimed that clean signals are wrong. With deadline propagation or cancellation, the debt does not exist and the first-attempt signal becomes the best input available. Nor has the trap condition been claimed as new. Bronson and coauthors’ own example already contains it. This post’s additions are the closed-form recovery time, the size of a trigger, and the condition under which a scaler holds a service in the trap.

Two open questions are named on purpose. Heavy-tailed service times and bursty arrivals could produce triggers of their own, and none of the models here can show it. And the trigger test proposed in this post is destructive by design and has not been run on a real service.

Two corrections follow from it. The first two posts of this series closed on the hope that a signal counting only what clients ask for would be the clean way out. This post shows where that hope fails, in the open rather than by quietly dropping it. And the rule of The Shared Ancestor Problem is confirmed rather than overturned: the independent signal failed for lack of power, the second of the two conditions that post stated.

What Is Left Open

The three signals differ in what they see, and they share what they do. Each one waits for the backlog to exist, then orders capacity for it, and the capacity arrives a dead time later. During that dead time nothing the autoscaler does reaches the service. The debt that decides the outcome is built in exactly that interval.

Every result in this series so far has treated the excess during the dead time as something the queue absorbs. The queue held all of it, and the controller’s only job was to catch up. A service has another option during that interval, one that does not depend on what the autoscaler can see. This post does not examine it.

Click a theme to branch it out and read its points. Each point shows the full path back to the root.

Demand Is Not Debt
Read the Cognitive Map as plain text

The Debt

  1. A request whose client timed out stays in the queue and is served for nobody. With R retries, every failing first attempt becomes units of work; a budget gives , and layers multiply.
  2. After a trigger pushes waits past the timeout, the failed state is permanent iff . Bronson and coauthors’ own example, stable below 150 of 300 queries a second with one retry, contains it exactly.
  3. With no trigger, request-level runs at from 1.5 to 2.85 ran 20,000 s without a single timeout. The second state exists and nothing shows it.

The Way Back

  1. Below the threshold, recovery after a k-fold spike of length takes about for a long spike: 2,400 s at 0.5, 3,750 s at 0.6, 10,500 s at 0.8, matched by fluid and request-level runs.
  2. The relaxation time grows as , the critical slowing that Safe in Probability, Not in Size described; at the service gains a permanent second state.
  3. Backoff delays retries without removing any, so A and the condition are unchanged; a five-second backoff left the trapped run trapped.

The Signal

  1. CPU recovers after 771 s at 12.5 times the needed pods; ingress rate after 266 s at 3 times; first attempts provision exactly the need and lose 99.7% of demand.
  2. A scaler on a debt-excluding signal holds ρ at its target, so it is trapped whenever the target is at least 1/A: any target of a third or more with two retries. At 33% it recovers after 8,909 s; at 25% after 384 s.
  3. The independent first-attempt signal cannot see the debt, which is part of the service’s state; the self-produced CPU signal can. A check needs both conditions The Shared Ancestor Problem named.

Compute it. Multiply your retry counts across every layer that retries to get A. If any layer uses a budget, use one plus the budget for that layer. Divide one by A. If your autoscaler scales on a signal that excludes retries, and its target is at or above that number, your service has a second state that a trigger can put it in. If your servers do not drop abandoned work, the same is true at fixed capacity whenever your utilization is above it.

Demand is what clients want now. Debt is what the service already agreed to do. An autoscaler that sees only the first will provision for a service that has paid its debts, and wait there, at exactly the right capacity, forever.

item.title: The Delay a Window Demands
item.author: Yuriy Polyulya
item.description:
Argument so far
  • One Bit per Dead Time's Proposition 2. A utilization metric saturates at the pods' allowance, so a controller scaling on it can at most multiply its ready pods by one growth factor per provisioning delay. It sizes an overload by probing, one round at a time.
  • The way out it pointed to. A signal that counts waiting work cannot saturate, so it sees the size of an overload at once. It is also driven by a backlog, and a backlog is a quantity that integrates past shortfalls.
  • What this post asks next. What does the provisioning delay do to a loop driven by a backlog, and what does a stabilization window, added to keep that loop calm, do to it?

A queue consumer is about the most natural thing to autoscale. Its work arrives as messages, its backlog is a number the broker already reports, and the obvious rule writes itself: one pod for every so many waiting messages. KEDA ships that rule for Kafka, for SQS, for RabbitMQ and for dozens of other sources. AWS documents the same idea for its own fleets as backlog per instance. It is one of the most common ways to scale asynchronous work.

Take such a consumer in a model. Each pod handles ten messages a second. Demand steps up to two thousand messages a second, which needs two hundred pods, and then stays there, perfectly flat, for twenty hours. The autoscaler aims for ten waiting messages per pod, the default threshold of KEDA’s Kafka scaler. A new pod takes 90 seconds to start consuming, and the Kubernetes autoscaler applies its default five-minute window to every scale-down.

Over the last hour of the run, with demand that never moves, the pod count does not settle. It spends most of the hour pinned at the configured ceiling of two thousand, ten times what the work needs. Then it falls to a handful of pods, as low as one, and climbs back. The fifth percentile of the hour is 8 pods, the ninety-fifth is 2,000, and the mean is 1,551.

The obvious suspect is the five-minute window, so remove it. The loop still swings from one pod to two thousand, with a mean of 936. Remove nothing, and instead raise the threshold until each pod’s share of the backlog is forty seconds of work. With the window, the loop still hunts, between 40 and 503 pods over the hour. Without it, the loop settles into a band from 186 to 234 pods.

So the window matters, but it is not the whole story, and removing it did not rescue the default. Something about a backlog-driven loop needs a standing quantity of waiting work to stay at rest, and the window raises how much. This post finds how much.

In brief
  • The belief. A stabilization window makes an autoscaling loop stable.
  • The mechanism. A backlog-scaled loop acts on the backlog of one dead time ago on the way up and, through the window, of one window ago on the way down.
  • The law. It rests only if every message waits a standing delay of at least : about one dead time at the default window, rising with the window, and never more than e dead times after an upward step. A closed form derived by harmonic balance gives the curve within 3.3% for windows from one dead time up to the default.
  • The bill. About ninety seconds of waiting on every message at a 90-second dead time, or a hunt that costs 17% to 99% more pods. The Kafka default supplies one second, and hunts with or without the window.
Notation used across the series

where:

  • - the dead time, from ordering a pod to its first served request; 90 seconds in the specimen
  • - the size of an overload, as a multiple of the load before it; when it is drawn at random
  • and - the utilization target and the utilization a service actually runs at
  • and - a pod’s CPU limit and CPU request
  • - the growth factor: the most the controller can multiply its ready pods by in one round
  • and - the downscale stabilization window, and the same window measured in dead times
  • , and - a backlog threshold in messages per pod, the rate of one pod, and the standing delay every message waits at rest
  • - the standing delay, in dead times, a backlog loop with window needs to rest
  • and - the retry amplification: units of work per first attempt once every attempt fails, and the same quantity whatever sets it, retry counts, budgets or limiters
  • , , and - demand, capacity, the client timeout and the length of a spike
  • and - a replica ceiling and an admission bound in seconds of capacity
  • L1 · Bound, L2 · Fit and L3 · Estimate - the tag on each claim: a proof or a cited fact, a judgment or approximation the text argues for, and a worked example computed from the model; each part’s ledger names the layer of every law it records

The Belief: the Window Makes the Loop Stable

L1 · Bound The Kubernetes documentation presents the stabilization window as the remedy for an unstable replica count. It names the problem first: “it is possible that the number of replicas keeps fluctuating frequently due to the dynamic nature of the metrics evaluated. This is sometimes referred to as thrashing, or flapping”[1] . It then gives the fix: “The stabilization window is used to restrict the flapping of replica count when the metrics used for scaling keep fluctuating.” With a five-minute window, the page explains, the controller “avoids having the scaling algorithm frequently remove Pods only to trigger recreating an equivalent Pod just moments later.”

L1 · Bound The default applies the window to scale-downs only. The documentation states it directly: “For scaling down the stabilization window is 300 seconds”, while “For scaling up there is no stabilization window.” KEDA, which turns a queue into a metric the Kubernetes autoscaler can read, passes the setting through untouched. Its specification says “KEDA would feed values from this section directly to the HPA’s behavior field,” and the example it prints sets stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300[2] .

The belief is reasonable, and for the loop the documentation has in mind it is correct. A noisy metric makes a ratio controller add and remove pods in quick succession. Each removal throws away a warm pod that the next sync will ask for again. A window that holds the highest recent recommendation stops that. It costs a few minutes of extra pods after every peak and buys a calmer count.

The belief carries an assumption it never states. It treats the window as a filter on noise, something that removes fluctuation without changing the loop it sits in. In a loop driven by a backlog the window is part of the dynamics. It holds pods after the work that justified them is gone, and holding pods drains the backlog the next decision will read.

How a Queue Reaches the Controller

L1 · Bound KEDA does not scale anything itself between one pod and many. It publishes each trigger as an external metric and creates a HorizontalPodAutoscaler that reads it. By default the metric has the type AverageValue, and KEDA’s specification spells out what follows: “If our metric is the queue size, the threshold is 5 messages, and the current message count in the queue is 20, HPA will scale the deployment to 20 / 5 = 4 replicas, regardless of the current replica count.”[2]

L1 · Bound The controller’s source agrees. For an external metric with a per-pod target, GetExternalPerPodMetricReplicas computes math.Ceil(float64(usage) / float64(targetUsagePerPod)), after the same tolerance check as every other metric[3] . The recommendation is the backlog divided by the threshold, rounded up. The current count enters only through the tolerance: if the backlog per current pod is within 10% of the threshold, the controller holds.

L1 · Bound That rule differs from the CPU path of One Bit per Dead Time in one decisive way. The CPU path counted ordered pods at zero usage, so it could not order the same capacity twice within a round. The backlog path has no such accounting. A pod that has been ordered but is not yet consuming does nothing to the backlog. The backlog keeps growing during the dead time, and the recommendation grows with it. The controller keeps ordering for work that the pods already on their way will eventually take.

One Sync, Walked Through

L3 · Estimate The port runs the external per-pod calculation on concrete inputs, with a threshold of ten messages per pod. The replica count is every pod the deployment has, whether it is consuming yet or still on order. Sweep the backlog for three replica counts.

L1 · Bound The three lines lie on top of one another almost everywhere. Two thousand messages at ten per pod is two hundred pods, whatever the current count, which is the rule KEDA describes. Each line leaves the shared diagonal only inside its own tolerance band. With two hundred replicas, any backlog from 1,800 to 2,200 messages holds the count at two hundred, and 2,300 messages asks for 230. The flat steps are the only place the current count matters. That has a consequence for the dynamics. Suppose a hundred of three hundred replicas are still starting. They have not touched the backlog, which has kept growing to four thousand messages, and the controller asks for four hundred. It has ordered a hundred more pods for work that the hundred already on their way will absorb when they arrive. The same line read downward is the other branch. A backlog drained to a thousand messages asks for a hundred pods, and only the window stands between that request and the count.

L1 · Bound The defaults set the scale of everything that follows. KEDA’s Kafka scaler takes lagThreshold, the “Target value for the total lag (sum of all partition lags)”, with a default of 10. Its SQS scaler takes queueLength, default 5, and its documentation gives the intended reading: “if one pod can handle 10 messages, set the queue length target to 10.” KEDA’s cooldownPeriod of 300 seconds “only applies when scaling to 0”. Between one replica and many, the Kubernetes autoscaler and its own window do the work.

L1 · Bound One more default bounds the Kafka case. Unless allowIdleConsumers is set, the Kafka scaler will not ask for more replicas than there are partitions, because a consumer beyond the partition count would sit idle. A Kafka consumer group therefore hunts, when it hunts, between one pod and its partition count. The model in this post has no partitions. Its ceiling is a replica limit of 2,000, which stands for whichever cap binds first in a real deployment.

L1 · Bound AWS documents a sizing rule for the same kind of loop. Its guide to scaling on an SQS queue defines backlog per instance and sets the target from the latency the application can accept: “take the acceptable latency value and divide it by the average time that an EC2 instance takes to process a message”[4] . With a ten-second acceptable latency and a tenth of a second per message, the target is a hundred messages per instance. This rule turns out to be the right one for choosing the threshold, for a reason the guide does not give. The next section shows why.

A Backlog Is an Integrator

Before the equations, one step worked through with numbers. Take a consumer of the size a test cluster can hold. Each pod handles ten messages a second, and demand steps from 50 to 200 messages a second, so the need goes from five pods to twenty. The dead time is 90 seconds, the window is the default five minutes, the replica ceiling is 100, and the threshold is KEDA’s default of ten messages per pod. At rest that threshold holds one second of work per pod.

L3 · Estimate In the first thirty seconds after the step the backlog reaches 4,700 messages, and the controller doubles its count at each of the two syncs, from five pods to twenty. By sixty seconds it has ordered 80 pods, and by ninety it sits at the ceiling of 100, five times the need, while only ten pods are consuming. The backlog keeps growing until the ordered pods start to consume, and at two minutes it still holds 14,850 messages. A hundred pods then clear it within a minute: 2,250 messages at 150 seconds and none at 180.

L3 · Estimate With the queue empty the recommendation falls to one pod, and the window holds the hundred pods for five more minutes anyway. When it lets go, the count drops at once to a single pod, and the backlog starts to build again from zero. The second climb begins from one pod instead of five, so it goes higher, past 24,000 messages, and from then on the loop repeats it exactly, every 510 seconds. Demand never moves after the step. The swing comes from three things the rest of this post takes apart: the backlog remembers every second of shortfall, the pods ordered against it arrive one dead time late, and the window keeps them one window too long on the way down.

The backlog changes at the rate work arrives minus the rate pods remove it. With demand , a per-pod rate c and N pods consuming:

The autoscaler sets N from L. The threshold T, in messages per pod, says how much backlog one pod should carry. At rest, with N pods exactly matching demand, the backlog sits at T messages per pod.

Definition 4 -- Standing Delay: the seconds of waiting a backlog-scaled loop holds at rest, which is the threshold per pod over the rate of one pod

Definition 4 (Standing Delay). A loop that scales on backlog with a threshold of T messages per pod, served by pods of rate c, holds at rest a backlog of T messages per pod. Its standing delay is

where:

  • - the threshold, in messages per pod
  • - the rate of one pod, in messages per second

By Little’s law, D is also the time every message waits in the queue at rest.

L1 · Bound At rest the backlog is , and Little’s law gives the wait as backlog over arrival rate[5] . That is , the standing delay. The threshold is a latency in disguise. The Kafka default of ten messages per pod, at ten messages a second per pod, is one second of waiting. The AWS rule, acceptable latency over time per message, sets the standing delay equal to the acceptable latency. The guide is choosing D directly.

L1 · Bound Strip the controller to its simplest form first. Suppose the pods consuming now are the ones the backlog asked for one dead time ago, . Write for the relative deviation of the backlog from rest. The backlog equation becomes

This is the linear delay equation with gain . The dimensionless product says how many standing delays fit in one dead time.

Proposition 3 -- Delay Equation Thresholds: the pure-delay backlog loop is stable iff the standing delay exceeds 2/pi dead times, and its characteristic equation has a real root iff the delay is at least e dead times

Proposition 3 (Delay Equation Thresholds). For with :

  1. The equilibrium is asymptotically stable if and only if , that is .
  2. The characteristic equation has a real root if and only if , that is .

Proof sketch. The characteristic equation is . For part 1, roots move continuously with a. As a tends to zero, one root tends to zero from the left and the rest have real parts tending to minus infinity. A root reaches the imaginary axis at only if and , which first happens at , so at . For part 2, a real root s satisfies , so s is negative. On the negative axis has its minimum at , so a real root exists exactly when .

L1 · Bound Part 1 of the proposition is the symmetric condition Anti-Fragile Decision-Making at the Edge used as a filter on actions, gain times delay below . That post applied it as a sufficient condition for a loop with one delay. For this equation it is also necessary. Part 2 is the stricter condition for a non-oscillating response, and it returns later in this post with a different job.

L3 · Estimate In the specimen’s terms, with a 90-second dead time, the pure-delay loop needs a standing delay above , about 57 seconds, to be stable at all. The Kafka default supplies one second. The pure-delay loop at the default is unstable by a factor of nearly sixty. That alone explains why the default hunts. It does not explain why the window makes things worse, or by how much, because the pure-delay model has no window in it.

L2 · Fit The reason a backlog loop needs a standing delay at all is the integrator. A backlog remembers every second in which capacity fell short and every second in which it ran over. A controller that reads the backlog through a dead time acts on a memory that is already out of date. The integrator keeps adding to the error while the correction is on its way. A larger threshold makes each pod’s share of the backlog larger, so the controller’s response to a given deviation is gentler. The standing delay is the price of that gentleness, paid by every message, all the time.

L2 · Fit The two loops in this series fail in opposite directions for one reason. The CPU loop of One Bit per Dead Time counted every pod on order at zero usage. It never ordered the same capacity twice, and it paid for that caution with a slow, fixed rate of learning when its metric saturated. The backlog loop learns the size of an overload at once, because its signal has no ceiling. It pays by ordering past the pods already on their way, since nothing in its signal says they exist. Both loops face the same dead time. One spends it waiting, and the other spends it accumulating a debt it will later overpay.

Two Branches, Two Delays

The deployed loop is not the pure-delay loop. Its way up and its way down pass through different mechanisms, and the difference is what the window adds.

L1 · Bound On the way up, a recommendation becomes capacity only after the dead time. A pod ordered now starts consuming 90 seconds later. If the recommendation dips in between, pods still starting are the first to go. The ReplicaSet controller ranks pods for deletion with unscheduled before scheduled, pending before running and not ready before ready[3] . So a pod reaches service only if it was wanted for the whole dead time without a break. The consuming count is the minimum of the recommendation over the last dead time.

L1 · Bound On the way down, the window holds the highest recommendation of the last W seconds, five minutes by default, and only then lets the count fall. A pod that is no longer wanted keeps consuming until the window has passed. The consuming count is the maximum of the recommendation over the last window, before the dead time’s minimum is applied to it.

Put together, and leaving aside the sync period, rounding and the tolerance, the loop is:

L2 · Fit While the backlog rises, the maximum does nothing, and the loop acts on the backlog of one dead time ago. While it falls, the window holds the old, larger value, and the loop acts on the backlog of one window ago. The way up has the dead time and the way down has the window. A window five minutes long on a loop whose dead time is ninety seconds makes the down branch more than three times slower than the up branch.

Physical translation. Picture a thermostat that switches the heating on a few minutes late and refuses to switch it off until the room has been warm for half an hour. In a room that loses heat slowly, nobody notices. In a draughty room the heating overshoots every time, then finally switches off, the room cools past the setpoint, and the late start overshoots again. The cure lies in the room rather than the switch: a room that holds more heat, with a reserve large enough that the two delays stop mattering. In a backlog-driven loop that reserve is the standing delay, and the window decides how large it has to be.

Definition 5 -- Hunting: a backlog-scaled loop hunts if a step in demand leaves a pod count that keeps swinging instead of settling

Definition 5 (Hunting). In the idealized loop, a loop hunts if the deviation produced by an upward step in demand, starting from rest, does not decay. In the deployed loop, measured over the last hour of a twenty-hour run, a loop hunts if its pod count swings by more than 30% of the pods needed.

The 30% threshold sits well above the ripple the 10% tolerance leaves in a settled loop, so tolerance ripple is not counted as hunting.

Proposition 4 -- Window Scaling Law: whether the backlog loop hunts depends only on the standing delay and the window, each measured in dead times; it rests iff D is at least tau times Phi(W/tau), a curve computed numerically

Proposition 4 (Window Scaling Law). In the idealized min-max loop, whether a disturbance decays does not depend on its size. Measured in units of the dead time, the only parameters are and . If, for each w, the gains at which the loop rests form an interval, as the integration finds for every w computed, there is a function of w alone such that the loop rests after an upward step if and only if

Proof. Around rest write . Both the minimum and the maximum commute with adding a constant, so the constant passes through them, and with . Both also commute with multiplying by a positive number, so F is positively homogeneous: if x is a solution, so is for every . Decay or growth therefore does not depend on the size of the disturbance. Rescaling time by leaves and as the only parameters. For each w, the integration finds a single critical value below which the loop rests and above which it hunts, and . The scaling is proven; the single crossing is observed numerically for every w computed, not proven.

L1 · Bound The scaling is exact for the idealized loop. It reduces a question with five parameters, demand, rate, threshold, dead time and window, to one curve of one variable. The curve itself has no exact closed form that this post could find. It is computed by integrating the idealized loop and bisecting on the gain, and two approximations derived below describe it to within a few percent.

The computed curve, with the two approximations derived later in this post and two reference lines:

L3 · Estimate The default case reads straight off the curve. A 300-second window over a 90-second dead time is w = 3.33, and . The loop needs a standing delay of about 82 seconds, nearly one full dead time. At w = 1 it needs 0.57 dead times, which is looser than the of the pure-delay loop. In the idealized loop a window as long as the dead time costs less than a pure delay on both branches would. Longer windows cost more, and the cost grows roughly with the logarithm of the window.

L3 · Estimate Short windows need very little. At a tenth of a dead time the idealized loop needs only 0.119 dead times of standing delay. With no window at all, it still rested at a standing delay of an eighth of a dead time, the shortest tested. The standing delay a backlog loop needs is created by the window, and the larger the window, the larger the delay.

What the Deployed Loop Does

The idealized loop has no sync period, no rounding, no tolerance, and no minimum or maximum. The deployed loop has all of them. The test is whether the curve still predicts where the deployed loop stops hunting.

L3 · Estimate The deployed model runs the ported external-metric calculation and the ported normalizer, with its stabilization window, every 15 seconds. The backlog is refreshed every 15 seconds. Demand steps from fifty pods’ worth of work to two hundred pods’ worth and stays there. The ceiling is 2,000 replicas and the floor is one, so a single pod is half a percent of the need and rounding does not pose as oscillation. For each pair of dead time and window, bisection finds the smallest standing delay at which the loop does not hunt.

L2 · Fit The deployed loop also samples. A change in the backlog reaches a decision up to one sync later, and a decision reaches the scale target at the next. The comparison adds a sampling delay of 10 seconds to both branches, so the effective dead time is and the effective window is . The 10 seconds is one value chosen for all sixteen pairs, not fitted pair by pair.

The observed boundaries, first against the window and then against the curve. Each comes from bisection over twenty-hour runs, with hunting as in Definition 5.

L3 · Estimate The curve carries over. Across dead times from 30 seconds to three minutes and windows from one minute to ten, the idealized law with one fixed sampling correction lands within 6% of the deployed boundary on average. The largest miss, 14%, is at the shortest dead time, where the 10-second correction is a third of the dead time itself and the sync period matters most. The misses are not random: all four larger than 10% overestimate the boundary, three of them at the two shortest dead times, so the correction is too large there. In every line of the first figure the boundary rises with the window. At a 90-second dead time, going from a one-minute window to a ten-minute one more than doubles the standing delay the loop needs, from 47 seconds to 98.

L3 · Estimate The opening’s puzzle now has its answer. With no window, the idealized loop rested at the smallest standing delay tested, but the deployed loop is never quite without a window. Its sampling adds about 10 seconds to the down branch, a window of a tenth of the effective dead time. The curve says that window needs a standing delay of 0.119 effective dead times, about 11.9 seconds. The deployed loop without a window hunts at a standing delay of 10 seconds and rests at 40, which is consistent with that prediction. Its band at 40 seconds, 186 to 234 pods, is a swing of 24% of the need. That is under Definition 5’s 30% threshold, though wider than the ripple of a loop well above its boundary. The default of one second sits far below either line, which is why removing the window did not save it.

L3 · Estimate With the default window the prediction is 89.6 seconds and the observed boundary is 85.5. A queue consumer at a 90-second dead time with the default window needs each pod to carry about ninety seconds of work before it will rest. Forty seconds, the opening’s second attempt, is less than half of that.

The boundary figures show where the hunt starts. The next figure shows its shape.

L3 · Estimate The hunting run is a regular cycle rather than noise, and each phase belongs to one branch. The plateau at 350 pods is the window holding a peak that the backlog no longer supports. During it, 350 pods drain a backlog that 200 could have held, so when the window lets go, the backlog is far below rest and the recommendation collapses. The rebuild then waits on the dead time, so the backlog overshoots again and the next peak is set. The cycle repeats every ten to eleven minutes for the whole hour, with demand perfectly flat.

L3 · Estimate The figure repeats the range of the hunt that the cost figure below gives as percentiles. What only the figure shows is that the hunt is a limit cycle with a fixed shape. Its longest phase is the window doing exactly what the documentation says it does.

The Window That Cannot Matter

The scaling law says the needed delay grows with the window. It does not say whether it grows without limit. A window of an hour, or a day, would by that reading demand an ever larger standing delay. A second result caps it.

Proposition 5 -- Window-Proof Delay: with a standing delay of at least e dead times, the loop recovers from an upward step without overshoot, so the window never acts, whatever its length

Proposition 5 (Window-Proof Delay). In the idealized min-max loop, let demand step upward from rest. If , the backlog rises monotonically to its new rest level without overshoot, the window never holds a recommendation above the current one, and the loop behaves exactly as the pure-delay loop does, for every window length. Consequently for every w.

Proof sketch. The step moves the rest level, not the backlog: L is continuous and equal to its old rest value for every time before the step, so in the coordinates of the new rest level the whole history, over the window and the dead time, is a constant , and the operator returns throughout the first dead time. While x is nondecreasing, the maximum over any window of x is its latest value, and the minimum over the dead time of a nondecreasing function is its value one dead time ago. So as long as x keeps rising, the min-max loop is the pure-delay loop . It remains to show that the pure-delay solution from a constant negative history keeps rising and never crosses zero when .

Write , so y starts at 1 and obeys the same equation. While y stays positive, let . Then . On the first dead time , so . If over the past dead time, then , and continuation carries the bound forward. A bounded keeps y positive, and makes it decrease to zero. So x rises monotonically to zero, the window never acts, and the loop rests. What Is Already Known

L1 · Bound Backlog per instance is documented practice, and so is the latency rule for choosing its target[4] . The guide also notes why a raw queue length is the wrong metric: “A policy that targets only the number of messages in the queue does not account for the number of instances available. As a result, it can add more instances than needed while the queue drains.”

L1 · Bound The distinction between a backlog signal and a rate signal is also known. KEDA’s RabbitMQ scaler offers both, a queue-length mode “to keep number of messages in the queue at selected, nominal level” and a message-rate mode “to keep the consumption rate up to messages publication rate”[2] .

L1 · Bound Instability from delayed queue feedback is long established in networking. Hollot and three coauthors analysed active queue management for TCP flows as a feedback loop with delay and designed controllers for its stability[7] . Johari and Tan studied end-to-end congestion control[8] . Delay limits its stability there too. Stabilization windows against flapping are documented by the controller’s own maintainers.

L1 · Bound Both effects of this post were met before, with physical servers and a 260-second setup time. Gandhi and three coauthors scaled up on the number of requests in the system, a backlog-type signal. They report that their policy “overshoots while scaling up capacity”, and that “a doubling of request rate can lead to a tripling of number of requests at a single server”[9] . That is the ordering past pods already on their way that the walked-through sync shows. For scaling down they made the servers “very conservative in turning servers off”, a delayed turn-off that is the stabilization window’s ancestor, and it helped a controller driven by request rate. The law of this post concerns the combination they did not study: the window in front of a loop driven by the backlog itself.

Exact Results for Setup Times

L1 · Bound Queueing theory has exact results for a close relative of this loop. Gandhi, Harchol-Balter and Adan derived them for server farms[10] . Their model is a farm of k servers with Poisson arrivals, exponential job sizes and an exponential setup time. Idle servers turn off at once, and every job not being served puts one server into setup. Their on-demand policy is therefore a backlog-scaled loop with a threshold of one job per server and no window. Their first theorem covers staggered boot, with at most one server in setup at a time. Response time is then exactly the response time of the same farm without setup plus one setup time, a decomposition they call “counter-intuitive since not all jobs will experience the setup time”. Their second gives the exact state distribution when the number of servers is unlimited.

L3 · Estimate Those results give the simulation machinery of this series an exact test. The check is a request-level simulation, with three seeds of 300,000 jobs each and time measured in mean job sizes. Across six configurations, three of each model, five of the six exact values lie inside the range of the seeds: at a mean setup of 1 in the staggered model, for example, the exact 2.205 sits between 2.195 and 2.221. The sixth, at a mean setup of 5, lies 1.7% above the seeds’ mean. Long setups make each busy period long, so a run of fixed length holds fewer of them. The seeds spread by 3% and 5% at setups of 5 and 10, against about 1% at a setup of 1. Where exact theory exists, the simulator agrees with it to within that noise.

L2 · Fit The exact theory and this post agree where they overlap, and they measure different things. Their models are stationary Markov chains. With no window, the on-demand policy settles at every load below capacity, as the idealized loop of this post rests without a window. In the staggered model the setup time costs every job one mean setup on average, an exact and modest price, and it never makes the system hunt. Hunting needs what those models leave out: a window that holds capacity after the need has passed, in front of a threshold that reacts through a fixed dead time. Their conclusion for the expensive corner is one this series shares: when both the load and the setup time are high, “it pays to leave servers on”.

L1 · Bound The idealized loop also belongs to a known class of equations. A differential equation whose right-hand side depends on the maximum of the unknown function over a past interval is called a differential equation with maxima. Bainov and Hristova collect the theory of that class[11] . The book gives existence results, integral inequalities and stability conditions of the Lyapunov and Razumikhin kind. The loop of this post nests a minimum over the dead time around a maximum over the window, and the scaling law, the ceiling of e and its exactness were derived here for that nested form directly. Whether the general theory already contains them, or yields a proof of the parts left open, was not settled for this post.

L2 · Fit Four results were not found in the sources read for this post. The first is the min-max form of the deployed loop, with its different delays on the two branches. The second is the scaling law that reduces its stability to one curve in the window over the dead time, checked against the deployed controller. The third is the window-proof delay of e dead times, its exactness as the least upper bound of the curve, and the latency floor that follows. The fourth is the closed-form harmonic-balance approximation to the curve and the logarithmic approach to e. They are offered as this post’s contribution, with the same caution as before: absence from the sources read does not prove nobody has written them down.

L3 · Estimate Noise widens the band without moving the boundary. Demand in the boundary runs is flat, so they were repeated with 10% demand noise, a multiplier redrawn every minute. L3 · Estimate A consumer-group rebalance is different. When the number of consumers changes, a Kafka group pauses consumption while partitions are reassigned. With a 10-second pause after every change, the loop still swung between 158 and 299 pods at a standing delay of 100 seconds, and rested between 186 and 206 at 150. With a 30-second pause it was irregular at 120 and 150 seconds, and rested at 200. A plausible reading is that the pause must fit inside what the tolerance band can absorb, roughly a standing delay above the pause divided by the tolerance. That reading is untested beyond these runs and is not part of the law.

L2 · Fit Several things are not in the model at all. The partition cap clips a Kafka hunt at the partition count. Activation from zero, which KEDA handles with its own cooldown, is not modelled. Neither are metric caching between the broker and the controller, visibility timeouts on SQS, or messages that fail and return to the queue. Each could shift the boundary. None is likely to remove it, because the integrator and the two delays are still there.

The Binding Constraint, in Sequence

L2 · Fit The Constraint Sequence Framework orders the constraints by which binds first. For a backlog-scaled consumer the dead time binds first, because it sets the unit in which every other delay is measured. The window binds second, because it sets how many dead times of standing delay the loop needs. The threshold binds third: it is where the needed delay is paid, and its value follows from the first two. The latency a team promises is the outside constraint the other three must fit under.

L2 · Fit The common response to a hunting consumer runs the sequence backwards. It lengthens the window to stop the flapping, which raises the delay needed, which makes the hunt worse at the same threshold. The sequence says to start from the dead time and then shorten the window to the shortest one that still serves its purpose. Only then does the threshold get set, from the curve, with a margin.

Falsification Criteria

Each criterion names an observation on a real cluster that would refute this post. All need a queue consumer scaled through KEDA on its backlog, with a measured dead time and a known per-pod rate c, so that the standing delay T/c can be set directly. The cluster kit for this series provides one. Its broker generates demand that steps from 50 to 200 messages a second, and each consumer takes ten messages a second after a 90-second start delay, so 20 pods are needed under a ceiling of 100. The predictions are the deployed model’s at that size, over the last hour of a twenty-hour run.

F1 (the boundary exists).

  • Condition: the default 300-second window, demand stepped up and then held flat, standing delays of 60 and 150 seconds, below and above the predicted boundary of about 90 seconds for a 90-second dead time.
  • Prediction: the first run hunts in a regular cycle; the second settles within the tolerance band. At the kit’s size the model gives 6 to 35 pods at 60 seconds and 19 to 21 at 150 seconds.
  • Refuted if: the loop settles well below the predicted boundary, or hunts well above it.

F2 (the window raises the boundary).

  • Condition: the same consumer at a fixed standing delay between the one-minute and five-minute boundaries, for example 60 seconds at a 90-second dead time.
  • Prediction: it rests with a 60-second window, between 19 and 22 pods, and hunts with a 300-second window, between 6 and 35.
  • Refuted if: the longer window settles the loop that the shorter one could not.

F3 (removing the window does not rescue the default).

  • Condition: the Kafka default threshold of ten messages per pod, one second of standing delay for these consumers, with and without the window.
  • Prediction: both runs hunt across the full range, from one pod to the ceiling of 100.
  • Refuted if: removing the window alone brings the loop to rest.

What This Post Did Not Claim

Where Each Claim Holds

Claim. The deployed backlog loop rests if and only if its standing delay is at least about .

  • Assumption: KEDA’s default AverageValue metric through the v1.34.0 controller on the default path, a fluid backlog, constant per-pod rate, and an upward step in demand.
  • Failure mode: a per-pod rate that falls with load, retries that return to the queue, or a partition cap below the need. Each changes the integrator or clips the swing.

Claim. The scaling law and the window-proof delay of e dead times are exact for the idealized loop.

  • Assumption: no sampling, rounding, tolerance, floor or ceiling, and an upward step from rest.
  • Failure mode: the deployed loop adds a sampling delay of about 10 seconds to each branch; the agreement in the boundary figures is evidence for the correction, not a proof of it.

Claim. Removing the window does not rescue a threshold far below the dead time.

  • Assumption: the controller’s sync and the metric refresh add a delay to the down branch.
  • Failure mode: none found in the runs; with no window the deployed boundary sat between 10 and 40 seconds of standing delay.

Reversal condition. The advice of this post is to treat the window as a cost and to size the threshold from the curve. It reverses when the backlog is not what the controller reads. A rate signal has no integrator in it, and a loop scaled on rate does not need a standing delay. That loop has a blindness of its own, which this post does not examine.

What Is Not Claimed

The laws in this post are exact for the idealized loop and checked, not proven, for the deployed one. The scaling of Proposition 4, the ceiling of Proposition 5 and its exactness in Proposition 5b are proofs. That the curve rises steadily between its two ends is observed, not proven. The curve itself is computed, its closed form is an approximation by harmonic balance, and its long-window form is fitted to a shape the argument only motivates. The sixteen deployed boundaries agree with the curve to 6% on average, and the four that miss by more than 10% all miss in the same direction.

It has not been claimed that stabilization windows are harmful. In front of a controller driven by a noisy rate, a window does what the documentation says, and Gandhi and coauthors found a delayed turn-off helpful for exactly that kind of controller. The claim is narrower: in front of a loop driven by a backlog, the window sets a price in waiting time that the documentation does not mention. Nor has it been claimed that KEDA’s defaults are wrong. Ten messages per pod is one second of waiting only for a consumer that handles ten messages a second. A consumer that spends ten seconds on each message carries a hundred seconds at the same threshold, and at a 90-second dead time it rests.

Three open questions are named on purpose. The limit of the curve at very long windows is argued, not proven. The second condition that consumer-group rebalances add is preliminary. And partition caps, metric caching and visibility timeouts are outside the model entirely.

Two credits belong here as well. The symmetric bound that Anti-Fragile Decision-Making at the Edge applied as a sufficient filter is also necessary for the pure-delay equation, which this post uses as its baseline. And the overshoot of a backlog-type signal during setup was observed with physical servers more than a decade before this series; this post adds its boundary, not its discovery.

What Is Left Open

A backlog sees the size of an overload, which the saturated metric of the first part could not. The price is that it remembers. Every second of shortfall stays in it until capacity removes it. A controller that reads it through two different delays needs a standing quantity of that memory just to rest.

Sizing the threshold correctly leaves one assumption standing. Every message in the backlog was waiting for a client who still wanted it. In the model, messages wait patiently for as long as it takes. Real requests time out, and real clients retry. A signal that counts only fresh demand avoids the backlog’s memory entirely. Whether it also avoids what the backlog was remembering is a question this post does not answer.

The Loop as It Runs

  1. The Kubernetes documentation presents the 300-second downscale window as the fix for flapping, and KEDA passes it straight through to the autoscaler.

  3. At rest every pod carries T messages, so every message waits seconds by Little’s law. The Kafka default of 10 messages per pod at 10 messages a second is one second. The AWS rule of acceptable latency over time per message sets D equal to the acceptable latency.

The Law

  1. Rising, the loop acts on the backlog one dead time ago; falling, the window makes it act on the backlog one window ago. The loop is .
  2. Both filters commute with shifts and positive scaling, so stability depends only on D and W in dead times: the loop rests iff . ; a closed form derived by harmonic balance is within 3.3% from one dead time up to the default window, and the deployed controller matches within 6% on average across sixteen dead time and window pairs.
  3. With the loop recovers from an upward step without overshoot, the window never acts, and so for every window. The ceiling is exact: below e some long enough window always makes the loop hunt, and with no window it rests at any delay.

The Bill

  1. Below the boundary the window holds every peak: at a 90-second dead time and the default window, mean pods run 17% to 99% above need, in a limit cycle about ten minutes long.
  2. At a 90-second dead time the boundary is 47 seconds with a one-minute window and 86 seconds with the default five. A latency target sized below cannot be held at rest.
  3. Sampling still delays the down branch by about 10 seconds, which needs about 11.9 seconds of standing delay; the one-second default hunts with or without the window.

Compute it. Measure your consumer’s dead time, from the scaling decision to the first message a new pod consumes. Add about ten seconds for sampling, and divide your downscale window, plus the same ten seconds, by that effective dead time. Read from the curve, or compute it: up to about three dead times use the closed form of Proposition 5a, which errs high by at most 3.3%, and beyond that use , which errs low by at most 2.7%. The product is the standing delay your loop needs. Divide your threshold by your per-pod rate. If the result is smaller, the loop will hunt, and the cheapest fix is usually a shorter window.

A stabilization window holds pods after the work that justified them is gone. In a loop driven by a backlog, that is the instability, and the threshold is where it gets paid.

item.title: One Bit per Dead Time
item.author: Yuriy Polyulya
item.description:
Every pod on the dashboard reads 100% CPU. The replica count says 20, then holds. Two minutes later it says 40 and holds again. Two minutes after that it says 80. Nobody has touched the autoscaler, and nothing is broken. It is doing what it was built to do, one step at a time. The engineer on call has one question the dashboard cannot answer: how much load is actually arriving?

The autoscaler cannot answer it either. That inability is the subject of this post.

The numbers above come from a model of an ordinary service, which this series calls the specimen and uses in all four parts. Ten pods sit behind the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, scaling on CPU at a 50% target. Each pod may use one core and serves a hundred requests a second at full use. A new pod takes 90 seconds from the order to its first served request. That is the provisioning window The Phase MAPE-K Usually Skips used for the time from a scaling decision to a new instance being live, kept here so the two results can be compared. Then traffic jumps to ten times its usual rate.

In that model the replica count roughly doubles every two minutes, from 20 to more than 300. Capacity catches up with demand after 345 seconds, and the count keeps climbing anyway, because a backlog piled up while capacity was short. It peaks at 317 pods, where 100 would have done the job.

Now the part that matters. Had traffic jumped to three times its rate instead of ten, the first two requests for capacity would have been identical: 20 pods, then 40. Had it jumped thirty times, the first five would have matched the tenfold run exactly. For the first several minutes of an overload, the controller’s behaviour carries no information about how large the overload is. It finds out only by adding capacity and watching what happens next.

The same pattern shows up in ordinary operations. A launch, a retry storm after a dependency recovers, or a batch job pointed at the wrong endpoint all produce it. The replica graph rises in stairs, each stair one provisioning delay wide. The usual reading is that the autoscaler is slow and needs tuning. This post argues for a narrower reading. The stairs are the controller measuring the overload, at a rate fixed by arithmetic that no setting in its policy changes.

In brief
  • The belief. A utilization metric measures load, and its target is a cost setting.
  • The mechanism. The Kubernetes autoscaler counts pods it has ordered at zero usage, so with a saturated metric one provisioning round can at most multiply its ready pods by .
  • The law. A k-fold overload needs at least rounds: 4 for a thirtyfold overload at a 50% target, 15 at the API default of 80%. At 91% and above, with the limit equal to the request, the controller never scales at all.
  • The bill. About two minutes per round in the specimen, an overshoot of 1.3 to 6.5 times the pods needed, and both worse when pods degrade under load.
Notation used across the series

where:

  • - the dead time, from ordering a pod to its first served request; 90 seconds in the specimen
  • - the size of an overload, as a multiple of the load before it; when it is drawn at random
  • and - the utilization target and the utilization a service actually runs at
  • and - a pod’s CPU limit and CPU request
  • - the growth factor: the most the controller can multiply its ready pods by in one round
  • and - the downscale stabilization window, and the same window measured in dead times
  • , and - a backlog threshold in messages per pod, the rate of one pod, and the standing delay every message waits at rest
  • - the standing delay, in dead times, a backlog loop with window needs to rest
  • and - the retry amplification: units of work per first attempt once every attempt fails, and the same quantity whatever sets it, retry counts, budgets or limiters
  • , , and - demand, capacity, the client timeout and the length of a spike
  • and - a replica ceiling and an admission bound in seconds of capacity
  • L1 · Bound, L2 · Fit and L3 · Estimate - the tag on each claim: a proof or a cited fact, a judgment or approximation the text argues for, and a worked example computed from the model; each part’s ledger names the layer of every law it records

What a Loop Cannot Know

This series takes one widely deployed autoscaler and asks four questions about it, one per part. Each question names something the loop cannot know from its own signal. Each part then prices the belief that lets engineers forget it.

  1. Size. A utilization metric cannot report more load than the pods can carry. What does the loop do when the load it must size exceeds anything its metric can show? This post answers that.
  2. Time. A loop driven by a backlog reacts to work that has already waited. What does a stabilization window, added to stop flapping, do to such a loop? Still open when this post ends.
  3. State. A demand-rate signal sees what clients ask for now. It misses the work that earlier requests left behind. When does that gap hold a service in a failed state? Also open.
  4. Where the excess goes. During the provisioning delay the replica count controls nothing. What bounds the damage then, and what does that bound cost? Also open.
